newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FEATURE-NZ's "clean" tourism industry losing shine.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-NZ's "clean" tourism industry losing shine.

text.p: Golden beaches, lush native bush, gushing rivers and snow-laden mountains -- it's a package that draws over a million tourists to New Zealand every year.
But beneath the "clean, green" image hides a tourism industry in disarray.

New Zealand's single largest foreign currency earner is in a trough, low-level corruption is rife and tourism operators say they're struggling to stay afloat as competition for the holiday-maker's dollar intensifies worldwide.

"There are a couple of emerging destinations which compete against us, South Africa and Canada in particular," said Jim Boult, managing director of listed tourism company Shotover Jet, which returned a NZ$3.92 million loss last financial year.
"In the last five years we've had roughly the same number of Germans come over here, but German departures to Canada have gone from 200,000 a year to 500,000 a year over the same period," he said.
"That's a hell of an increase. It shows you that with the right marketing and the right packaging, the business is there."
NEW ZEALAND'S GROWTH FIGURES HALVED
But New Zealand isn't getting it. Growth in the number of people visiting the country has more than halved since the industry's heyday in the early 1990s.
In the year ended June 1997, 1.54 million visitors arrived in New Zealand, up five percent on the previous year, but a far cry from the peak of 14.5 percent growth in 1993.
The New Zealand Tourism Board has had to rethink its target of three million visitors to the country by the year 2000, and acknowledges that the industry is facing a critical period.

"What we've had since 1991 is a large increase of players in the tourism industry because of the boom that's been going on, and I think as a result of that, quite a few people are finding it hard to maintain their market share," said Chris Ryan, the Tourism Board's deputy chief executive.
LOSING THE MARKETING PLOT?
The problem has been amplified by a change in the nationalities visiting New Zealand. Boult said New Zealand had "lost the plot" in a number of its key markets.
"What we've seen happen in New Zealand in the last couple of years is a lot of our longer stay visitors have disappeared -- that's (from) the U.S. and Japan in particular.
"They are a far smaller percentage of the people coming here than they were. That's been replaced by, say, Korean and Taiwanese visitors, who come in for three or four nights.
"So our bed night numbers have contracted somewhat over the past couple of years, and that's certainly hurting," he said.
The tight market has spawned the widespread use of kickbacks -- payments demanded by tour guides and bus drivers from tourism outlets in return for a group's patronage.

Tourism outlets have traditionally paid small commissions to secure business, but increased competition and the entrance of South East Asian operators working on tight margins has created a cut-throat environment where everybody fights for a cut.
In Queenstown, the mecca of New Zealand tourism in the South Island, kickbacks are reportedly as high as 30 percent. Some outlets refuse to grease palms, but lose money for their morals.
And the level of the corruption is said to be on the rise.
Tour guides, particularly those from South Korea, have been accused of charging tour parties commissions on activities that are free or have already been paid for, such as shopping and trout fishing.
In March, police detective inspector Graham Bell alleged some guides were charging their clients a non-existent "departure tax" to cross the Cook Strait, which separates the North and South Islands.
The Tourism Board concedes that the bad will created by kickbacks and excessive commissions has the potential to destroy New Zealand's reputation and its competitiveness.
LIGHT ON THE MILLENNIUM HORIZON

The board is also concerned about falling yields -- that is, tourists staying for shorter periods and spending less -- and is in the process of devising a five-year plan to take the industry into the next century.
And some are optimistic that the industry, worth NZ$4.8 billion ($3.1 billion) annually, will blossom once again.

The high value of the New Zealand dollar had been a major hurdle for all New Zealand exporters, not least tourist operators. Its dramatic fall against the greenback in recent weeks is a correction that the industry has long been hoping for.

Also awaited with great anticipation is the turn of the century, when New Zealand will be one of the first nations to see the new millennium's first dawn, which the industry believes could provide it with a much needed shot in the arm.
